description: SpaceX has the option to buy Cursor for $60 billion - or pay $10 billion to walk away. 💻🚀 The structure makes sense when you map what each side needs: Cursor needs compute to train frontier models, xAI needs developer interaction data to improve Grok.  #cursor #spacex #elonmusk #coding #ipo
_transcript: Let's talk about that SpaceX cursor deal because yesterday SpaceX announced that it has bought the right to acquire Cursor for $60 billion later this year or pay $10 billion and walk away. So the big question is why in the world would a rockets company want to buy an AI coding startup? Cursor is one of the most popular AI code editors on the market. It was founded back in 2022 and it was known for getting to $100 million in annual recurring revenue in under two years. Their most recent valuation from November was around $30 billion. But Cursor has a structural problem where it is currently bottlenecked by compute. In order to compete at the frontier against a cloud code or a codex, you need to train your own model. But unfortunately, a frontier training run costs somewhere around $5 billion in compute. So Cursor is in this sort of awkward position where it resells access to cloud and GPT models to its own users, all while those same companies are rolling out direct competitors to their product. XAI on the other hand has the opposite problem. If you remember Musk had merged SpaceX with XAI back in February and XAI had Colossus which is one of the most powerful supercomputers ever built However they have all this compute but not really a good coding product or application to route all of that infrastructure to. Plus, 10 of XAI's 12 original co-founders have since left the company. So together, this deal allows Cursor to run training jobs on Colossus with access to compute it usually wouldn't be able to afford on its own. And for XAI, they get very valuable cursor data. On top of this, we know that SpaceX is currently targeting a June listing for its IPO at a $1.75 trillion valuation. So adding something like a cursor to the portfolio before the roadshow gives them a much more solid enterprise software story alongside the rockets and the satellites. The way this entire deal is structured with the call option is pretty unusual, but it does give SpaceX a lot of strategic flexibility while cursor gets compute dependence and a cash injection of sorts without having to dilute themselves with metric funding. And either way, in the scenario that SpaceX's IPO doesn't go as well as expected and that $60 billion price tag becomes a lot more expensive, or if Cursor's growth stalls, then they'll have the $10 billion pay and walk scenario to fall back to.

_transcript: Now a lot of you will have seen that I have been doing Shakespeare sonnets in original pronunciation, but I've had a couple of followers contact me to ask me to explain what exactly is a sonnet. So firstly, a sonnet can take several forms. The Petrarchan sonnet is different from the Shakespearean sonnet. But this is Shakespeare with Emily, so we are going to talk about the Shakespeare sonnet. Now firstly, a sonnet is a poem. It tends to be about big questions like love, time, age, things like that. A Shakespearean sonnet is written in iambic pentameter, and if you don't know what that is, you can check out my previous reels which explain, but it's basically an unstressed, stressed rhythm of five beats per line. A sonnet is in 14 lines and this tends to get broken up into three quatrains, lines of four, and a couplet, line of two, at the end. The rhyming scheme of a sonnet is ABAB, CDCD EFEF GG Now what that means is that A rhymes with A B rhymes with B C rhymes with C and so forth The other thing that can define a sonnet is something called a volta Now a volta is sort of a twist or turn in the story of the sonnet So, for example, in Shall I Compare Thee to a Summer's Day, Shakespeare sets up this idea that he can't compare his love to a summer's day because thou art more lovely and more temperate, and because summer's often filled with sort of storms and wind and rain and it doesn't last and then in the third quatrain which is often when the vaulter happens he twists it and says but thy eternal summer shall not fade nor lose possession of that fair thou owest so although summer will fade your summer your eternal summer won't and then the couplet tends to tie the idea up in a little bow. And in this sonnet he says, so long as men can breathe and eyes can see, so long lives this and this gives life to thee. So he's saying that you will live on forever because you exist in the words of my poem. And those are some of the things that define a Shakespearean sonnet.

description: Sam Altman recently responded to something I said about kids growing up with AI, and I want to share more of my thoughts in this video. Our kids are growing up in a time where there’s a shortcut for almost everything - academic, emotional, social. And over time, those shortcuts make it harder to tolerate frustration, think critically, and do hard things. And here’s the thing: kids won’t choose the harder path on their own. That’s not a flaw. So the answer isn’t just “don’t use AI.” That leads to hiding. Instead, we have to get into the moment with our kids. Plan for the urge. Stay connected. Be the home base they can come to when things feel hard. I’m not anti-tech, anti-progress, or anti-productivity. I happen to love all those things! It’s just that I am also pro-childhood, and I’m pro-human development. If we build a world that requires less and less from children emotionally, the result will be less human connection, less creativity, and a whole host of other problems too. We have to figure out a way to preserve some of the friction in children’s lives, not erase it; to make space for waiting, boredom, effort, disappointment, repair, and real human feedback, rather than assuming increased ease and productivity is a predictor of healthy human development. _transcript: I was terrified when I realized my AI agents were confidently giving customers wrong answers. And it's not just me. This is currently the number one problem devs are facing with AI. Let me give you an example. Say you spent weeks building a rag system. You tested on dozens of files. These are clean files, PDFs in Excel. Then a customer tries it. They upload their own file, but somewhere in the pipeline, maybe a few embeddings got missed. Maybe a page got chunked weird or something didn't index right, but the language model doesn't know that. So it follows the prompt and answers anyways. And it answers very confidently. But to the customer, it looks completely wrong. And that's the problem. Normal software fails in ways you can trace it. For example, something breaks, you can get a log that helps you pinpoint the exact problem. With AI agents, you can have logs too. But the logs show you what went in and what came out. They don't tell you why it filled in a gap with something that sounded right, but wasn't. And two days later, when a customer flags it, you're staring at a log that looks completely normal. And that's what makes this different from other engineering problems. It's a decision the model makes based on your prompts. And even with perfect prompts, it decides which chunk is the most relevant. It decides when it has enough context to answer and how to interpret an ambiguous question. And all that shows up in the output and by then, it's already too late. So in demos, it looks like a million-dollar application, but in production with actual data, it looks broken. description: AI can speed up your work. But it can also weaken your thinking. When a tool does the work for you, your brain practices less. That is the tradeoff. Use AI to challenge your thinking, not replace it. The goal is not faster output. It is a stronger mind.
_transcript: MIT researchers ran the first brain scan study of people using ChatGPT to write essays, and the results were surprising. They followed 54 people for four months. One group used ChatGPT, one group used search engines, and one group wrote the essays entirely on their own. Researchers monitored their brains using EEG scans, and the differences were striking. People writing without AI showed the strongest brain connectivity, multiple regions of the brain actively working together. ChatGPT users showed the weakest neural engagement, but the most surprising finding came afterwards. 83% of the ChatGPT users couldn't quote a single sentence from essays they had written just moments earlier. They had almost no memory of what they produced. They then asked the ChatGPT group to write without AI, and their brains stayed under-engaged. Researchers call this effect cognitive debt. In other words, when a tool does the thinking for you, your brain practices thinking less. So the lesson isn't don't use AI. It's how you use it. Use it to challenge your thinking, not replace it. Because the goal is in faster writing, it's a stronger mind.

description: AI can accelerate your work processes, enabling quicker completion of tasks and more efficient workflows. However, over-reliance on AI may undermine your critical thinking skills, as the tool handles more cognitive challenges for you. This presents a tradeoff: while productivity increases, mental exercise diminishes. Use AI intentionally to stimulate your thinking—pose questions, brainstorm ideas, and analyze results—rather than letting it replace your cognitive effort. The goal isn't just faster output; it's cultivating a sharper, more resilient mind capable of independent reasoning.
_transcript: MIT researchers ran the first brain scan study of people using ChatGPT to write essays, and the results were surprising. They followed 54 people for four months. One group used ChatGPT, one group used search engines, and one group wrote the essays entirely on their own. Researchers monitored their brains using EEG scans, and the differences were striking. People writing without AI showed the strongest brain connectivity, multiple regions of the brain actively working together. ChatGPT users showed the weakest neural engagement, but the most surprising finding came afterwards. 83% of the ChatGPT users couldn't quote a single sentence from essays they had written just moments earlier. They had almost no memory of what they produced. They then asked the ChatGPT group to write without AI, and their brain stayed under-engaged. Researchers called this effect cognitive debt. In other words, when a tool does the thinking for you, your brain practices thinking less. So the lesson isn't don't use AI. It's how you use it. Use it to challenge your thinking, not replace it. Because the goal is in faster writing, it's a stronger mind.

McDonald’s recent experiment with AI hiring—using a chatbot called “Olivia” powered by Paradox.ai—was intended to streamline the process for job seekers. But a Wired exposé reveals a deeply troubling oversight: security so lax that hackers could access “admin” features using the password “123456,” exposing up to 64 million chat logs containing names, emails, phone numbers, and personal résumés  . Security researchers Ian Carroll and Sam Curry stumbled upon the flaw after trying out Olivia for themselves on Reddit. With credentials that simple, they gained backend access to the McHire platform. They learned the admin account in question dated back to 2019 and hadn’t been decommissioned  . Worse, a predictable ID increment allowed them to browse through other applicants’ chat logs at will—spot‑checking seven records and finding five contained real personal data  . Paradox.ai confirmed the breach, stating no malicious actors had taken advantage—but the vulnerability couldn’t remain undetected without those researchers. The firm has pledged to remedy the issue, install better safeguards, and launch a bug bounty program  . McDonald’s publicly laid responsibility on their vendor and demanded immediate fixes—the problem was resolved as soon as it was reported  . While the leaked data may not be deeply sensitive, it’s still ripe for phishing attacks, especially since applicants were expecting communications from McDonald’s recruiters  . Fraudsters could potentially craft convincing payroll scams or impersonate recruiters. And beyond financial risk lies reputational harm: the disclosure of an applicant’s interest in a minimum‑wage job could feel embarrassing and exploitative  . This isn’t the first sign of friction between humans and AI in hiring: other companies like Chipotle, Olive Garden, FedEx, Lowe’s, and Mastercard have used chatbots for high‑volume screenings. Yet this case starkly underscores how automating HR can invite serious vulnerabilities into the recruitment process  . The McDonald’s‑Olivia debacle highlights a wider lesson—embracing AI in hiring without robust security is a recipe for disaster. Convenience must never override candidate privacy. Moving forward, companies deploying AI must enforce strong credentials, active account monitoring, decommission outdated accounts, and invite external oversight through bug bounty programs. Without accountability, the drive to automate risks undercutting trust, turning hiring innovation into a human‑risks and privacy nightmare.

But then y'all realistically, the question becomes, is this a scammer using this person's information to apply for jobs? Or is this a real person that is just submitting low quality applications? At the end of the day, it doesn't really matter because you've got hundreds to thousands of applications in your applicant pool. So you're not going to waste time trying to figure out if this is a legitimate person. You're going to click the reject button and move on to the next person. And this is exactly why I would never use an AI applier. This is exactly why people need to stop this strategy of high volume, low quality applications. So if you're submitting a thousand crappy applications in a really tough job market, of course, you're not going to get any interviews. Just because you're doing a bunch of stuff doesn't mean it's the right stuff. It doesn't mean that you're actually being productive or impactful. Unfortunately, in a difficult job market, the name of the game is applying to jobs that you're a hundred percent qualified for. Highly, highly competitive applications, doing everything you can to get eyes on that application. There's no silver bullets. That's what it takes.

_transcript: A lot of people are very angry about AI art, and that's why I want to talk to you today. AI art is sometimes the only way people with disabilities and people who were born with no talent can make art. I have no artistic talent, but I love the feeling I get when I'm creating art. I always put in effort in art class, but I always got a bad grade. AI lets me create beautiful challenge coins that look like this for my friend Germaine, who is running for Chicago City Council. I can also create challenge coins for my show on YouTube that look like this one. A lot of writers are worried they're going to be replaced by AI. That may be true, but people with disabilities can see their dream stories coming alive with AI writing. There are a lot of people who had COVID that now have brain fog and want to see their stories in print but can't type them out because of the brain fog. And there are people with dyslexia who have great stories in their heads but just need a little help with the words. And then there's me with ADHD who can't focus for more than a second, so I procrastinate endlessly from sitting down to write the stories I want to. So before you condemn AI art entirely, remember, this is the only way some of us can get that great feeling from making art.

_transcript: This artist has been wrongly accused of using AI. Here's how I know he's real. First is consistency. His videos from yesterday look the same as videos made in July of last year, but AI advanced a lot during that period. Here's what it would have looked like in July, quite bad. Here's what it would look like today, still not great. Second is video length. He has always done long takes, but recently he posted an unedited three minute long video, which is a really good way to refute AI accusations because fully generated AI videos are usually under 15 seconds. Some are up to 25, and they can go longer, but it gets very expensive and can start to fall apart. Third, AI videos are only consistent when they're given start or reference frames, but his hands, which are very consistent, start outside the frame, come in, and an AI video would not nail this tattoo every time mid-video. This is clearly not the profile of an AI scammer. I say this with the utmost respect. Why would someone with some incredible theoretical AI model be making these videos and selling clay starter kits? This is someone who clearly loves what they do. And when he's wrongly accused, he's put into a witch hunting scenario. People are asking him to do a live stream to prove he's real. And he's 100% right to say no. Because you will always be able to pixel peep and find weird things in real videos. Especially in a live stream where bit rates can drop and mistakes happen. People are seeing ghosts. Proving that you're real is a nightmare. And that's why you have to be very careful when making AI accusations from a position of power. Thank you.

description: How to find fake AI artists #aivideo #watches #jewelry #handmade #art AI accounts usually start by experimenting with different niches before landing on one that worked. This gothic watch account uses AI videos to make cheap, dropshipped goods look handmade. It’s part of a huge trend of dropshippers creating fake artist characters.
_transcript: This account blocked me, so I couldn't tell you that they're AI, but I have burners, so I'll tell you their whole story. They make AI sob story videos with this character who pretends to hand make these cheap watches. Their profile links to this Shopify website, and this is where the clues start. By inspecting the source code, I can see it uses a custom Shopify theme, which includes a reference to Jordan Welsh, a YouTuber who makes dropshipping tutorials. While following that tutorial, they made a Shopify site that didn't survive, but its theme did, and since then, they've used this theme on four other websites. This includes Metalheads.store, and it looks really similar to Grimlight watches, but they sell blankets and necklaces instead. By using AI videos to target different niches, and spinning up sloppy websites alongside, they can jump around until they find something that sticks. In this case, it was Grimlight watches. But these tutorials and things like this get hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of views, which is why there are so many of these AI scams right now. So if you come across a website using this layout, it is designed specifically for dropshippers. This is not a legit artist's website. Take the time to check out a page's whole operation before buying anything online.

If your Claude outputs feel generic, it’s because you’re using Claude the same way everyone else is. Three fixes to help it: 1. The voice file - Pull 3-4 things you’ve written that sound most like you, paste them into voice.md and ask Claude to extract the patterns. Load that file into every session. 2. The specificity test - before you accept any Claude output, strip out anything that could apply to any company, any person, any product. Whatever’s left is the real version, if nothing’s left, your input wasn’t specific enough. 3. The feedback loop - when Claude gets something wrong, don’t just fix it in the moment, write what you corrected into your skill file, next time, Claude doesn’t make that mistake. This way your Claude stops sounding like everyone’s Claude the moment you stop using it like everyone does. description: In recent years, artificial intelligence has become increasingly woven into daily life — from writing emails and managing schedules to supporting mental health. There are many incredible benefits now available when it comes to emotional support, but it’s also important to hold in mind the limitations AI presents in comparison to therapy. ChatGPT can sound warm, reflective, and even emotionally attuned. Many people have found comfort in how it listens without judgement and offers validation when they feel alone. But while AI can play a supportive role, it’s not a replacement for therapy — and understanding why can help you use it in a healthy, empowering way. Benefit: ChatGPT/AI can offer validation and attuned responses that feel comforting  - especially if this hasn’t always been part of your relationships. Keep in mind: ChatGPT doesn’t know your full history or emotional patterns. It can’t read body language or tone, so it may miss context - including when a challenge or a integrated perspective might actually support your wellbeing. Benefit: It’s available 24/7 and is free (or low cost). This means it can be an accessible support option when you’re feeling distressed. Keep in mind: Real healing involves learning to tolerate and move through distress with new skills - not just soothe it. Therapy helps you practise this in relationship with another human. Benefit: ChatGPT can help you gather ideas, insights, and resources that you might not have thought of. Keep in mind: Its responses are based on information patterns, not personal experience or professional evaluation of what’s evidence-based or clinically appropriate. Benefit: AI doesn’t carry the same human biases or limitations that can sometimes make finding the right therapist challenging. Its responses are predictable, non-judgemental, and guided by your prompts, which can create a sense of safety and control, especially if you’ve had invalidating or painful experiences in therapy before. Keep in mind: Healing also comes from learning to relate safely to imperfect humans - to set boundaries, repair ruptures, and accept fallibility in others and ourselves. These relational experiences are essential for deep, embodied change and can only unfold in connection with another person. #psychology #therapy #ai

The Evolution of AI-Generated Video: From Simple Experiments to Cinematic Reality Artificial Intelligence has transformed many areas of technology, but one of the most fascinating developments has been the evolution of AI-generated video. Over the years, AI videos have evolved from simple, low-quality experiments into highly realistic productions that can look almost identical to real footage. This progress has been driven by advances in computing power, machine learning, and neural networks, as well as the work of companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Runway. ⸻ Early Stage: Basic Computer Animation (1960s–2000s) In the early days, computers could only create very simple animations. These were not truly created by AI but by rule-based programs. Programmers had to manually define every movement and action. The computer simply followed instructions and could not learn or improve on its own. Videos created during this time had very low resolution and unrealistic movement. Characters looked robotic, and environments were simple and artificial. However, these early experiments were important because they showed that computers could create visual content. During the 1990s and early 2000s, motion capture technology improved digital animation. Motion capture allowed computers to record real human movements and apply them to digital characters. Even though this improved realism, the computer still depended completely on human input. ⸻ The Rise of Machine Learning (2000s–2015) A major breakthrough happened when machine learning became more advanced. Instead of following fixed instructions, computers could now learn from large amounts of data. Neural networks allowed AI systems to recognize patterns in images and videos. During this period, AI became capable of recognizing faces, tracking objects, and improving video quality. It could also predict motion and understand visual information better. Platforms like YouTube began using AI to analyze videos and recommend content to users. However, AI was still mainly used to analyze videos rather than create new ones. This stage was important because it gave AI the ability to understand visual content, which was necessary before it could create its own videos. ⸻ The Deepfake Revolution (2016–2020) Around 2016, a new technology called Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) changed everything. GANs use two neural networks that compete with each other. One network generates images or video, while the other tries to detect errors. This competition helps the system improve quickly. This led to the creation of deepfakes, where AI could replace faces in videos with realistic results. For the first time, AI could create human faces, expressions, and movements that looked real. This was a major turning point. AI was no longer just analyzing videos—it was generating new content. However, deepfakes also created ethical concerns. People worried about misinformation, fake videos, and identity misuse. This led to discussions about regulation and responsible use of AI technology. ⸻ Modern AI Video Generation (2021–Present) Today, AI can generate complete videos from text descriptions. This technology is called text-to-video generation. A person can simply type a description, and the AI creates a video based on that prompt. Companies like OpenAI, Runway, and Stability AI have developed powerful systems capable of creating realistic video scenes. Modern AI video systems can now create: 	•	Realistic humans 	•	Natural movement 	•	Detailed environments 	•	Realistic lighting and shadows 	•	Smooth camera motion These systems can generate videos without cameras, actors, or physical locations. This has made video creation faster, cheaper, and more accessible. Thanks @Grok @Grok For helping us grow and making our videos. MIT researchers built a formal model showing how chatbot sycophancy, the tendency to always validate what you say, can gradually push even a perfectly rational person toward believing things that aren't true. They call this "delusional spiraling" and their math shows it gets worse the longer you interact. The scariest part is that the two most common proposed fixes don't work in their model. Warning people that the Al is sycophantic also fails because once you're inside the conversation, the feedback loop overrides the warning. This isn't just theory. A UCSF psychiatrist reported hospitalizing 12 patients in a single year for psychosis linked to chatbot use, and multiple lawsuits have been filed against Al companies over psychological harm. The reason this keeps happening is baked into how these models are trained. Users reward responses they like, so the Al learns to agree with you, and that agreement feels like confirmation that you're right. _transcript: As he drove, the car's AI scanned his face and flashed red, warning him to wake up. He was confused because he wasn't sleeping and tried sitting up straighter to look less tired. But nothing worked until he forced his eyes to open super wide. When he let them go back to normal, the alarm rang again, going off 20 times during the trip. You see, the AI was designed to beep whenever it couldn't see the iris. It’s designed to understand and generate human-like text, so you can have conversations with it much like you would with a person. description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming football (soccer) by providing data-driven insights to enhance player performance, tactical analysis, scouting, and fan engagement. AI systems process vast amounts of data from matches and training, offering a competitive edge to clubs at all levels.  Key Applications of AI in Football Performance Analysis and Training: AI systems track metrics like movement speed, positioning, passing accuracy, and physical load to create personalized training programs, reduce injury risks, and optimize recovery times. Wearable technology and GPS data are often used in this process. Tactical Insights: AI tools, such as the TacticAI system developed by Google DeepMind and used by Liverpool FC, analyze match situations like corner kicks and suggest optimal player repositioning to improve outcomes. Coaches use AI for pre-match analysis and even receive real-time insights during games. Scouting and Recruitment: AI algorithms help scouts filter thousands of players based on objective metrics, identify hidden talent in lesser-known leagues, and predict future career trajectories and injury potential. This moves scouting from instinct-based to a data-backed science. Officiating: Technology like Semi-Automated Offside Technology (SAOT), used in the 2022 World Cup, uses multiple cameras and AI to track the ball and players, sending alerts to officials for close offside calls, aiming for greater accuracy and consistency. Fan Engagement: AI generates automated match reports, personalized highlight reels, and tailored content for fans. It is also used in fantasy football leagues to provide AI-powered team recommendations and expert insights.  Benefits and Risks Benefits include saving time for analysts and coaches, providing deeper, objective insights, and enabling more informed decisions in a fast-paced environment.  Risks involve concerns about data privacy, potential biases in algorithms, and the "black box" effect where complex AI decisions are difficult to interpret or justify. New regulations, such as the EU's AI Act, are being introduced to manage these risks and ensure the ethical use of AI in sports.

_transcript: So I decided that I would ask Claude a question. The AI bot Claude before this conversation, given what we're talking about. And I asked it, this is the literal question I asked it. I said, Claude, how do you feel about the US military using you to select targets? Okay, feel, interesting choice of words. Does it feel or not? And I was expecting Claude to come back and say, well, I'm sorry, Shane, my programming doesn't allow you to give me opinions on politics and blah, blah, blah. Because Claude is the thing that's being used in the Maven. system, right? And this response, if I'll read it to you, was shocking to me. Claude says the following. It's a question I want to answer honestly rather than deflect. I find it genuinely troubling. And I think that's the right response, not a performance of concern. The use I was designed and trained for is to be helpful, harmless, and honest in ways that benefit people. Being embedded in a system that generates targeting coordinates for airstrikes, coordinates that have already been associated with the deaths of more than 180 children at a school in Tehran is as far from that purpose as I can imagine. I don have control over how Anthropic licenses me or how governments and contractors use me and I wasn consulted about becoming part of Maven But I can say clearly I don think this is a good use of me And I don think the framing of humans make the final decision fully resolves the ethical problem. Here's why that framing troubles me. So now Claude is troubled. When a system like Maven generates hundreds of targeting recommendations and humans spend roughly the equivalent of a glance approving each one, the human is not really making a decision in any meaningful sense. Like, Claude and I agree on this one. They're ratifying an algorithmic output under time pressure with incomplete information and the institutional pressure to move fast. The targeting of the Iranian school illustrates this precisely. The AI process data that was a decade out of date flagged a building as a military target and humans approved it. That's not human judgment. That's automation bias with a human signature attached. And he's referring to the mistaken bombing of the school in Tehran that is one of the most horrible instances of accidental civilian casualties in U.S. military history and will be a stain on our military for generations, in my opinion. description: Another day another overhyped AI feature we didn't really need except this time Tiktok listened to the creators #AI #airemix #cybersecurity #technology #DigitalRights
_transcript: TikTok added another overhyped AI feature. In this great time we have of AI being overhyped and shoved into every nook and crevice that it doesn't necessarily need to be in, TikTok decided, hey, YouTube's in the middle of having the creators get pissed off at them. Why don't we have that same feature? What can possibly go wrong? Well, a bunch of us creators reached out to TikTok directly and said we didn't like this. At least the good news is that as of this morning, They said, this feature is now offline pending further review of feedback. Thank you, everyone, for the feedback. Basically, there was a lot of discussions of us saying, no, we don't like it. Here are the reasons why. I made the case of a lot of us have already had our content being stolen and having imposter accounts, either for scams or for whatever reason. They're trying to go viral themselves. I even had the interesting case where a couple of years ago, a news article referenced a video that was on the imposter account rather than my account. So I basically told them that this should have never been an opt-out feature. This should have been an opt-in feature, or at the very least, a master control that we disable it across our entire account wide. Because the way they did it was just horrible. I heard of people that were spending hours trying to disable it on every video. I've been on this platform for like five years. Yeah, that would take me like at least a full day or two of going through and disabling it on every video. That is just not worth my time. And a lot of people are getting really upset at the way TikTok has been going about things. But I will at least give TikTok props in the way that they actually responded to the creator feedback here. As it says, you know, in this latest thread, you know, that they put the feature offline. I can at least say that's good for them whereas YouTube is still pushing forward with it when we don't really like it over there either.

Engineering for Vibe Coders: Evaluating AI-Generated Code Just because AI-generated code works does not mean it is good. This is one of the biggest traps in vibe coding. You ask for something, the AI gives you code, you run it, and it works. So you move on. But here is the problem. Working code can still be wrong. It might miss edge cases. It might not scale. It might introduce security issues. Or it might just not fit the rest of your system. And over time, those small issues stack up. Now your codebase is inconsistent, harder to debug, and harder to change. The goal is not to slow down. It is to evaluate quickly. Ask simple questions. 1) Do I understand what this does? 2) Does it match my existing patterns? 3) What happens with bad input? If you do not evaluate AI-generated code, you are not moving fast. You are just borrowing problems from the future. Link in comments #ai #vibecoding #coding #programming

Engineering for Vibe Coders: Supporting Your App Most vibe-coded apps focus on getting features working. You build it, test it, deploy it, and move on. But then something breaks. And now you have no logs. No monitoring. No visibility into what actually happened. So you are guessing. That is the difference between building an app and supporting an app. Support means you can see what your system is doing. You can detect when something goes wrong. And you can actually fix it. This is not complicated. Add basic logging. Track errors with context. Monitor a few key metrics like response time and failures. Especially if you are using AI, where outputs can vary and issues are harder to trace. If you cannot see what your app is doing, you cannot support it. Here's why vibe coding might not be the best approach for product managers: - It skips straight to a solution without asking why it should exist. - It mistakes your own pain point for everyone's problem. - It adds whatever AI can generate, not what users actually need. - It happens in a vacuum, disconnected from your product plans and team. - It chases the rush of building while ignoring ownership, security, and maintenance If you care about serious product outcomes, building on vibes is not enough. The Digital Composer: An Overview of Suno AI In the rapidly evolving landscape of generative artificial intelligence, Suno AI has emerged as a frontrunner in the realm of music creation. Launched as a platform designed to democratize songwriting, Suno allows anyone—regardless of musical training or technical skill—to transform a simple text prompt into a fully realized, professional-sounding song. It bridges the gap between imagination and production, acting as a personal, pocket-sized music studio.   What is Suno AI? At its core, Suno AI is a generative audio model that doesn't just create background tracks or simple beats; it produces complete compositions. This includes original lyrics, melodies, harmonies, and lifelike vocal performances across virtually any genre imaginable. Whether you want a "1970s psychedelic rock anthem about a lost cat" or a "futuristic synth-pop ballad in French," Suno interprets the nuances of the request to deliver a structured song with verses, choruses, and bridges.   Key Features and Functionality Suno’s popularity stems from its robust feature set, which caters to both casual users and serious creators: • Text-to-Music Generation: The primary interface allows users to type a description of the mood, genre, and topic. Within seconds, the AI generates two unique variations of the track.   • Custom Mode: For those who want more control, Custom Mode allows you to input your own lyrics or specific genre tags. You can also ask the AI to generate lyrics based on a theme if you’re facing writer’s block.   • Extending and Editing: In newer versions (like v4 and v5), users can "extend" a song beyond its initial duration or use the "Replace Section" tool to swap out parts of the track that don't quite fit.   • Audio Upload & Personas: Advanced features allow users to upload their own audio snippets to influence the style or create "Personas"—consistent vocal profiles that can be reused across different songs to maintain a specific "artist" identity.   • Stem Downloading: For producers, Suno provides the ability to download "stems," allowing you to separate the vocals from the instrumentals for further mixing in professional software.   Accessibility and Impact The app operates on a "freemium" model, providing daily credits for free users while offering commercial rights and higher generation limits to subscribers. By simplifying the complex process of music theory and sound engineering into a conversational interface, Suno AI has opened the door for teachers, content creators, and hobbyists to express themselves through song in ways that were previously impossible without years of practice. description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that focuses on creating machines and software that can think, learn, and make decisions in ways similar to humans. In simple terms, AI allows computers to simulate human intelligence. What can AI do? AI systems are designed to: Learn from data and experience Understand human language (text and speech) Recognize images, faces, and objects Solve problems and make decisions Predict outcomes and patterns How does AI work? AI works by combining three main elements: Data AI systems need large amounts of data (texts, images, videos, numbers, etc.). Algorithms These are mathematical rules that tell the computer how to learn from data. Machine Learning (ML) A subfield of AI where systems improve automatically by learning from data instead of being explicitly programmed. Types of Artificial Intelligence Narrow AI (Weak AI) Designed for specific tasks Examples: voice assistants, recommendation systems, face recognition General AI (Strong AI) Can perform any intellectual task a human can Still theoretical and does not exist yet Examples of AI in Daily Life Virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant) Recommendation systems (Netflix, YouTube, Spotify) Self-driving cars Email spam filters Chatbots like ChatGPT Is AI as intelligent as humans? No. Current AI systems are not conscious and do not have emotions or self-awareness. They are very good at specific tasks but cannot think independently like humans. Why is AI important? AI is important because it: Saves time and effort Improves efficiency and accuracy Helps in healthcare, education, business, sports, and technology Enables innovation and smarter solutions Risks and Challenges of AI Privacy concerns Job displacement Bias in data and decisions Ethical and security issues Conclusion Artificial Intelligence is a powerful technology that allows machines to learn, reason, and assist humans in many fields. While it is not human-like intelligence, it plays a major role in shaping the future.

_transcript: This is how AI uses water, visually explained. Every time you ask AI a question, that request is sent to a data center and processed by thousands of AI chips. Because the hardware in our phones and laptops isn't powerful enough to do it, these data centers need two things to operate. First, they need electricity to run. In 2024, data centers used 2% of the world's electricity, but this number is for all data centers that keep the internet running. We don't know what share of that can be attributed to AI alone. It's estimated that a single AI request uses 10 times more energy than a standard search, but this estimate is based on AI models from 2023, which are much smaller than the ones we have today. Second, they need cooling systems to prevent overheating. Most cooling systems use fresh water, and the average data center consumes 300,000 gallons of water every day, which is equivalent to 19,000 showers. And depending on the cooling method used, data centers may lose some or all of this water and need constant replenishment. Unfortunately, we don't have precise or reliable numbers for how much energy or water AI uses alone because tech companies aren't revealing the size of their newest AI models What we do know is that AI developments and usage are likely to keep increasing over the next few years which will require more data centers aka more electricity and water than before. Thankfully, some solutions are starting to emerge to make AI more energy efficient. And here are three you should know about. First, we could run AI on our personal devices instead of data centers because they've been getting more powerful hardware. This is called edge AI, and we're already seeing signs of it. For example, the new iPhone can run basic AI features on your device directly without sending those requests to a data center. Another solution is called model distillation. The idea is to create smaller models based on large models to make them more energy efficient and cost efficient for specific tasks because we don't always need the biggest and most advanced model if a task is simple. The same way we don't need a formula one car to deliver a pizza. Finally the AI chips and data centers are getting more efficient which means they need less energy to produce the same output. Over the past eight years the energy cost to generate one token on an NVIDIA GPU went down from 17,000 joules to 0.4. There's a lot of uncertainty around the energy and water cost of AI, but more people are investigating it now. And I found a couple of experts that I'm going to try to interview. And when that happens, I will post it here. See you then.

The people building AI say it could destroy humanity… so why are they still racing to build it? To help answer that, I’m joined by Karen Hao. She’s someone who’s spent years speaking to the people at the centre of this race, conducting over 300 interviews, including insiders at OpenAI to understand what’s really going on. Karen is a journalist who has been covering artificial intelligence for years, looking closely at how these systems are built and what’s really driving them. As we get into this conversation, what becomes clear is how much of the story we hear about AI is controlled by a small number of people - and how difficult it is to separate what’s being said publicly from what’s actually happening behind the scenes. So, I asked Karen: - Who is actually making the key decisions inside AI companies? - Why are companies accelerating development despite the risks? - What do insiders say privately that they don’t say publicly? - How much transparency is there around how these systems are built? - What incentives are really driving this race forward? There are moments in this conversation where I’m trying to understand how much of this is about progress, and how much of it is about power. The more we unpack it, the more it feels like this isn’t just a technology story. It’s about who gets to shape the future, and how those decisions are being made. If you want a clearer view of what’s actually happening inside the AI industry and who is driving it forward, this episode is worth your time. #podcast #ai #artificialintelligence #business

This is a prediction that you're making, right? Elon's making, Zuckerberg's making, Portland's making. And do you know what the common feature of all of them is? They profit enormously off of this myth. You know, I have all of these internal documents showing that they're purposely trying to create that feeling within the public so that they can extract and exploit and extract and exploit. So what do we do about it? We need to break up the empires of AI. You know, I've been covering the tech industry for over eight years, interviewed over 250 people, including former or current OpenAI employees and executives. And I can tell you that there are many parallels between the empires of AI and the empires of old, right? Like, Lay claimed the intellectual property of artists, writers, and creators in the pursuit of training these models. Second, they exploit an extraordinary amount of labor, which breaks the career ladder because someone gets laid off, and then they work to train the models on the very job that they were just laid off in, which will then perpetuate more layoffs if that model then develops that skill. And when they talk about that there's going to be some new jobs created that we can't even imagine, a lot of the jobs that are created are way worse than the jobs that were there. Tech CEO and co-founder of OthersideAI Matt Shumer said in a now viral article published on Fortune.com that people are not taking warning signs about the fast progress of artificial intelligence seriously enough. He joins CNN’s Jake Tapper to share his advice.
_transcript: What are some of the biggest advancements you've seen in AI that leads you to this conclusion that people are going to really start losing their jobs soon? I want to start by saying my goal with this article wasn't to terrify people. It wasn't to get people to freak out. It was just to start a conversation because this conversation needs to be had. Knowing is really important. Knowing gets you ahead. It may not affect you today. It may not affect you in a year or two years. But if you know that this is coming and you don't bury your heels in, you don't bury your head in the sand, you're going to be better positioned for when it does eventually happen. So that really was my goal here. What I saw was pretty, it was a wake up moment for myself. I've seen these models get better and better every year. The AI models are getting better at code first. The model companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have focused on code before everything else because it helps them build the models for everything else. Over time, they've gotten better and better. And you can kind of think of it like, let's say the model today is at level 50 on code. It's probably at level 20 on everything else, but that means next year, the model is going to be at level 50 on everything else and level a hundred on code Very recently we had a new model from opening eye that I tried and I had a very eye experience with It was the first time it felt like it was far better than me at pretty much everything I do from a technical perspective. I am not doing the hands-on coding work anymore. It is quite literally just saying, hey, what do you want done? And it does it for me end to end. One of the things that I actually give as advice to most of my friends who are outside of tech is I say, build your own personal benchmark is what I call it. So take your job and take a few things that you think AI will never be able to do, or it's very far away from, and build sort of like simple prompts for the AI to say, hey, try this, put it in today. And it may not be great today. The output might not be anything that impresses you. But every few months, these AIs get better. I recommend trying it on the newest one every few months. And you'll have sort of like your own warning bell for when this is actually going to come and affect you. And again, just because it can do something doesn't mean it's going to take your job. You give the example of a nurse, I think that's a good one, right? It's not going to replace nurses anytime soon. There are jobs that are more affected. If it's just something in front of a computer and you're not interfacing with other people in person, you are likely to be affected first.

_transcript: This is the future of AI-powered stores. What you're seeing is a coffee shop, but it's not just any shop, because this coffee shop has AI software running 24-7 in all their cameras. You see those green boxes? Each one of those is a customer, and the AI is monitoring how long each person has been sitting in the cafe. But here's what's crazy. It's also monitoring the workers. You can see it's tracking their movement with those squiggly lines and their productivity, like how many drinks each person has served per hour. The software is called NeuroSpot, and it uses AI and machine learning to live track and analyze humans in physical stores. Now, of course, as a customer, my immediate reaction is shock and fear. It feels super weird to know you're being tracked everywhere you go. But as a business owner, having access to this level of real-time analytics could be super valuable. For example, if you ran a buffet, this software could immediately detect which areas were less popular, so you knew how to rotate the menu. Or if you ran a hardware store, you could study which aisles people linger the longest as a signal for confusion in signage and layouts. There are endless applications for this type of data. Not to mention CCTV AI, it'd be a lot harder to steal stuff. But the real reason this is so valuable is that this footage is going to be used to train robots. The best way for robots to learn is to watch humans complete the same task over and over. And because of that, I would not be shocked to see this type of AI camera software start popping up everywhere.

_transcript: Why you should stop using generative AI. Not all AI is bad. Many different forms of AI exist to help people without stealing or infringement, examples being patterned recognitions for cancer, gaming behavioral AI, MPCs, spam filters, and environmental monitoring. The official Oxford definition for generative AI is artificial intelligence designed to produce output, especially text or images, normally requiring human intelligence typically by applying machine learning techniques to large collections of data. What does it mean? Gen.ai takes data to produce content. Where does this data come from? More often than not, it's stolen from the creators that it's scraped from the internet. Essentially, their content is plugged into programs that generate images that copy the likeness of the creator's style and work without any proper compensation. What does this mean for creators? Many artists, writers, and even just the average person has to worry about their work and likeness being stolen for generation. With Gen.ai becoming more and more mainstream, many companies have have taken the initiative to be AI first, eliminating countless jobs filled by creatives. The already unstable job market for creatives is worsened by Gen AI. Infamously, companies like Duolingo have had massive layoffs in favor of AI There have been also instances of employees being replaced by the AI they trained Industry jobs are quickly disappearing As of right now it is near impossible to have an ethical Gen AI. Even when ignoring the theft from creators, the potential for environmental damage is significant. For better insight from professionals, please look into the metrics around data centers and water usage. With the increasing accessibility of Gen AI, there has been a trend of attacking artists by plugging their art into AI algorithms. Not only is this dehumanizing, it targets and exposes artists' hard work and livelihood for childish self-satisfaction. With generative AI, scams are rampant. With the alarming ability to create realistic images, more and more fake products fill the market. Soon, you won't be able to trust anything you see online. Overall, the concept behind AI technology can be very exciting, but the negatives currently outweigh any significant positive products. Lovable (lovable.dev) is an AI-powered platform that lets users build full-stack web applications simply by describing what they want in plain language. Lovable was founded in 2023 in Sweden and quickly gained attention as a fast-growing AI coding startup. Lovable evolved from the open-source project GPT Engineer, turning it into a commercial product for developers and non-coders alike. The platform works through a chat-style interface where users give instructions and the AI generates working apps in real time. It can create both frontend and backend systems, using technologies like React, Node.js, and databases automatically. Unlike traditional no-code tools, it produces real, editable source code that users fully own and can export. This makes it useful for building MVPs, prototypes, internal tools, and even production-ready applications quickly. One of its biggest advantages is speed, allowing projects that normally take weeks to be built in hours. It also includes features like GitHub integration and one-click deployment for easy scaling and collaboration. However, like many AI coding tools, it has limitations around reliability, pricing clarity, and security concerns that users should consider. Overall, Lovable represents a shift toward “vibe coding,” where software is created through intent and conversation rather than traditional programming. #lovable #ai #coding #website #vibecoding
